title: Differentiability of the shape function in the planar corner growth model

source.title: Differentiability of the shape function in the planar corner growth model

notes: The paper is available as [arXiv:2611.33433](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33433). The map follows the final draft selected on 23 November 2026. Certificate coverage refers to the reviewed formalization of 24 November 2026.

Sections 4, 6 and 7 present bounded-weight arguments; Appendix B supplies the general-weight forms used for the full theorem. Conditional claims retain their stated premises. Heuristics and conjectures are identified separately.

results.label: Theorem 2.1
results.title: The shape is differentiable
results.summary: For independent, identically distributed, nonconstant weights, $g$ is differentiable throughout $\mathbb R_{>0}^2$ if the negative part has a finite moment of some order greater than one and the positive part has a finite moment of some order greater than four. Atoms and signed weights are allowed.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Theorem 2.2
results.title: Where the shape equals the largest weight
results.summary: For a finite largest possible weight $M$, the weighted and top-indicator shapes have exactly the same flat directions. The theorem classifies this set below, at and above the oriented site-percolation threshold, and proves differentiability at its critical point or endpoints.
definitions: Here $M$ is the smallest real number with $\mathbb P\{\omega_0\le M\}=1$, $p=\mu(\{M\})$, and $g_{\rm top}$ is the directional shape for weights $\mathbf1\{\omega_z=M\}$. A direction is $\xi=(t,1-t)$ with $0\le t\le1$.

In the top-site model a site is open when $\omega_z=M$. The critical probability $p_c$ is the infimum of the independent open-site probabilities for which an infinite up-right open path from the origin has positive probability.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Lemma 2.3
results.title: Two linear bounds for the shape
results.summary: The left and right derivatives of the concave shape give two linear upper bounds for $g$. Both touch $g$ at the chosen interior direction, and each approximates $g$ to first order from its own side.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.

coverage.scope: Both supporting bounds, their contact with the shape and their signed one-sided first-order errors are certified on the closed nonnegative quadrant.

results.label: Lemma 4.1
results.title: High-weight paths near a prescribed segment
results.summary: Between any deterministic endpoints separated on scale $s$ and staying away from the coordinate directions, a path has weight close to $g$ of its displacement and stays close to their straight segment, with probability tending to one. The probability estimate is uniform over the permitted endpoint pairs.
definitions: The scale $s$ tends to infinity. Both the permitted loss in weight and the permitted distance from the segment are fixed positive multiples of $s$.

coverage.scope: One scale cutoff and one probability bound work for all deterministic endpoint pairs permitted by the statement; both path clauses hold on the same path.

results.label: Lemma 4.2
results.title: High-weight paths for all endpoint pairs
results.summary: With probability tending to one, every point in one specified level interval can be joined to every point in a later interval. All joining paths stay close to their straight segments and collect nearly the shape-predicted weight, on the same event.
definitions: A level interval consists of the lattice points on $z_1+z_2=I$ between two specified endpoints, for an integer $I$.

coverage.scope: All allowed endpoint pairs are connected on one common event. Both the bounded and general-weight proofs are covered.

results.label: Proposition 4.4
results.title: Paths rarely exceed either linear bound
results.summary: For either supporting linear function, the probability that a path in a strip of width proportional to $s$ exceeds that linear value by $εs$ tends to zero as $s→∞$, uniformly over every positive integer path length.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.

coverage.scope: The probability limit is uniform over every positive integer length. The real-centre extension is recorded separately at Remark 4.6.

results.label: Lemma 5.1
results.title: Raising finitely many weights at small probability cost
results.summary: A small independent chance to replace each weight by the maximum of itself and a fresh sample raises weights at a controlled probability cost. Outside a small exceptional set of starting values, each selected weight has a uniformly positive chance of a definite increase.

coverage.scope: The same maximum-resampling law supplies monotonicity, the product density, the squared density bound and the independent positive boosts on the selected set.

results.label: Lemma 5.2
results.title: Crossings of length ⌈s³⌉ become unlikely
results.summary: Outside the directions supported entirely by sites of largest weight, a strip of width proportional to $s$ and length $\lceil s^3\rceil$ becomes unlikely to contain a crossing whose weight is within a fixed multiple of $s$ of the shape prediction.
definitions: The scale $s$ tends to infinity. A crossing joins the two end levels of the strip and stays inside it; its starting point may vary within the first level.

coverage.scope: The full cubic-length crossing estimate is certified outside the top-indicator flat segment, including the free starting point and strict weight threshold.

results.label: Proposition 5.3
results.title: The length where crossing probability becomes small
results.summary: A crossing with nearly the shape-predicted weight is likely at lengths comparable to the strip width. The first power-of-two length where its probability drops below a fixed threshold grows faster than the width and is bounded above by the cube of the width.

coverage.scope: The certificates cover the short-length probability bound and the first dyadic characteristic length, including its minimizing length, divergence and cubic upper bound.

results.label: Lemma 5.4
results.title: Infinitely many scales with comparable earlier lengths
results.summary: Infinitely many strip widths have crossing lengths that remain comparable to those at earlier widths. This selects scales where connections built at several smaller widths can be combined without their available lengths decreasing too quickly.

coverage.scope: The infinite selected set satisfies the printed comparison at every permitted earlier index, including the current index.

results.label: Lemma 6.8
results.title: Paths between prescribed grid points
results.summary: For bounded weights, one event supplies connecting paths between all prescribed grid points, with a common weight and location bound. Remarks 6.9 and 6.10 give the eligible random-endpoint form and its probability bound for general weights.

coverage.scope: The bounded statement uses exactly the specified common event. Remarks 6.9 and 6.10 record the separately certified general-weight path and probability clauses.

results.label: Proposition 6.11
results.title: An upper weight bound for every path in a rectangle
results.summary: With probability tending to one, every directed path in a prescribed large rectangle has weight at most a supporting linear value plus a small multiple of the rectangle's width. Both endpoints may be chosen after the weights are observed. The result holds under the full moment assumptions.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.

coverage.scope: The full endpoint rarity limit is certified for bounded and unbounded signed weights. The general proof uses eligible staircase windows and bounded endpoint trimming.

results.label: Lemma 7.2
results.title: Paths containing no rare subpath
results.summary: A full stage containing none of the counted high-weight subpaths cannot exceed either supporting linear bound by much. If it ends because it reaches the length threshold before the width threshold, its weight lies strictly below the average of the two supporting values.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.
Fix $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$ with $0<\xi_1<1$. Put $r(z)=z_1-\xi_1(z_1+z_2)$; this measures displacement from the line in direction $\xi$.

A stage ends when a path first reaches $2n_*$ steps or changes its $r$ coordinate by at least $s_*$. Here $n_*,s_*>0$ are fixed length and width scales. A stage ending at one of these thresholds is full; the final shorter piece is a remainder.

The counted subpaths either exceed one of the two supporting linear bounds by $\eta s_*$, or cross a specified strip of length $n_*$ and half-width $8s_*$ with weight greater than $n_*g(\xi)-Ks_*$. Here $\eta,K>0$ are fixed constants. Disjointness concerns collected vertices, so a terminal vertex may be shared.

coverage.scope: The bound holds for both supporting functions. A full longitudinal stage also has the stated positive loss relative to their average.

results.label: Lemma 7.4
results.title: Weight bound from a count of rare subpaths
results.summary: For bounded weights, a stage's weight is bounded using the number of disjoint subpaths that exceed a supporting bound or make a nearly shape-weight crossing. A large excess in the stage's weight therefore requires many such subpaths.

A stage ends when a path first reaches $2n_*$ steps or changes its $r$ coordinate by at least $s_*$. Here $n_*,s_*>0$ are fixed length and width scales. A stage ending at one of these thresholds is full; the final shorter piece is a remainder.

Here $\eta,K>0$ are fixed constants. Disjointness concerns collected vertices, so a terminal vertex may be shared.

coverage.scope: The source maximum over disjoint witness families is attained on the tested stage and gives the printed weight bound.

results.label: Proposition 7.6
results.title: Long paths contain few rare subpaths
results.summary: At a suitably chosen fixed scale, almost surely every sufficiently long path from the origin has fewer than $\lfloor N/32\rfloor$ counted subpaths with disjoint collected vertices, where $N$ is the number of its full stages. The assertion holds simultaneously for all such paths.
definitions: Fix $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$ with $0<\xi_1<1$. Put $r(z)=z_1-\xi_1(z_1+z_2)$; this measures displacement from the line in direction $\xi$.

Here $\eta,K>0$ are fixed constants. Disjointness concerns collected vertices, so a terminal vertex may be shared.

coverage.scope: The printed strict integer bound holds eventually on one probability-one event for every path from the origin, with the actual stage maxima and remainder.

results.label: Lemma 7.7
results.title: Path-weight bounds when the shape has a corner
results.summary: If the two one-sided slopes of $g$ differ, each full stage contributes a positive loss relative to the average supporting function. The number of counted high-weight subpaths controls the possible offsets. Summing this estimate gives the bounded-weight contradiction that rules out a corner of $g$.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.

A stage ends when a path first reaches $2n_*$ steps or changes its $r$ coordinate by at least $s_*$. Here $n_*,s_*>0$ are fixed length and width scales. A stage ending at one of these thresholds is full; the final shorter piece is a remainder.

Here $\eta,K>0$ are fixed constants. Disjointness concerns collected vertices, so a terminal vertex may be shared.

coverage.scope: The full-stage and whole-path inequalities use the stated multiplicities and include the final remainder.

results.label: Lemma A.1
results.title: A boundary circuit around a finite lattice set
results.summary: Every finite connected set of lattice sites has a surrounding square-boundary circuit. Its forward and backward sides mark at least a quarter of its length, control the enclosed area, and admit the stated finite counting bound.

coverage.scope: All five clauses are certified for an arbitrary finite connected signed-lattice set and marked site, including both quarter-perimeter label bounds and the circuit count.

results.label: Lemma A.2
results.title: An infinite up-right path through likely events
results.summary: Events indexed by lattice sites admit an infinite up-right path through successful sites with positive probability, provided failures are uniformly sufficiently unlikely and events at well-separated sites are independent. The path starts at the origin, whose event must also succeed.

coverage.scope: The certified high-density path begins at the origin and includes its event. The proof uses the separately certified contour with the printed dependence and count bounds.

results.label: Lemma A.3
results.title: Probability bound for disjoint path events
results.summary: For any finite list of high-weight path events, requiring the paths to collect disjoint sets of vertices has probability at most the product of the separate probabilities. The weights may have any real-valued distribution; the terminal vertex of each path is excluded from its collected set.

coverage.scope: The finite path-family inequality is certified for arbitrary real-valued independent weights and disjoint collected vertices. Its finite-chain proof is an approved alternative to the draft quantile-bit proof.

results.label: Lemma B.1
results.title: A lower bound for selected path weights
results.summary: Choose finitely many paths using only the information of which sites satisfy $\omega_z<-T$, and require them to avoid collecting those sites. The lemma bounds the probability that any chosen path has a very negative weight. This permits path selection to depend on the locations of unusually negative weights.
definitions: The threshold $T>0$ is fixed. Path selection may use all indicators $\mathbf1\{\omega_z<-T\}$ but no further weight values. Collected vertices exclude the terminal vertex.
The region $F$ is fixed before observing the weights; it must contain the collected vertices for every possible outcome, rather than only the paths observed in one outcome.
Here $N$ and $n$ are fixed nonnegative integers bounding the number of selected paths and their lengths.

coverage.scope: The entire bad-site mask may select the finite path family. The count-tail and Bernstein terms hold at the printed thresholds, with the same bound after finite-region exhaustion.

results.label: Lemma B.3
results.title: Paths joining every pair of endpoints
results.summary: Lemma 4.2 has the same simultaneous endpoint and path-location conclusion under the general moment assumptions. All permitted endpoint pairs are connected on one event whose probability tends to one.

coverage.scope: The simultaneous endpoint statement is certified under the appendix negative-moment and integrated square-root positive-tail assumptions.

results.label: Lemma B.4
results.title: Short paths reaching prescribed points
results.summary: Every point of a level interval can be joined by a short path to one of a suitably spaced finite set of points on a later level, with high probability. All these paths have a small lower bound on their weight. A corresponding construction works in the reverse direction.
definitions: A source level interval is a finite interval of lattice points with $\ell(z)=I$, where $I\in\mathbb Z$. A target set consists of deterministic lattice points on level $I+m$, where the integer $m\ge1$ is the required path length. “Prescribed” means chosen before observing the weights.

coverage.scope: Every prescribed finite net satisfying the stated spacing and count conditions is covered. A common positive lower bound tends to one for both forward and backward events.

results.label: Lemma B.6
results.title: Paths can go around the very negative vertices
results.summary: With probability tending to one, the obstructions created by very negative weights occur in bounded groups. Paths can then follow a prescribed direction while avoiding those weights, with uniformly bounded displacement from the line. The same construction supplies the endpoint adjustments needed to join these paths to crossings.

coverage.scope: The same event controls its probability and all five deterministic clauses in the specified region and collars. Both forward and backward reach estimates use the current contour lemma.

results.label: Lemma B.7
results.title: A lower weight bound for many chosen paths
results.summary: A family of short paths may be chosen after observing the locations of very negative weights. If it avoids those sites, the probability that any member has an excessively negative weight tends to zero, even when the number of candidate paths grows polynomially with the scale.

coverage.scope: The stated lower-weight bound holds simultaneously for every mask-measurable avoiding family with the permitted polynomial count and path-length bound.

results.label: Lemma B.8
results.title: Large positive weights do not spoil the connections
results.summary: The positive moment assumption controls very large weights throughout the regions used for connections. Requiring each trial rectangle to contain no such weight still leaves a fixed positive crossing probability, and the crossing events in disjoint rectangles remain independent.

coverage.scope: The global upper cap and all coarse trial caps have the stated uniform probability limits. The capped trials have probability at least half the crossing threshold and are jointly independent.

results.label: Lemma B.9
results.title: The path bounds with unbounded weights
results.summary: The stage and whole-path estimates remain valid for weights without a uniform upper bound after adding an explicit correction for the weight collected above a chosen threshold. This separates the contribution of individual large weights from the number of counted high-weight subpaths.
definitions: Fix $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$ with $0<\xi_1<1$. Put $r(z)=z_1-\xi_1(z_1+z_2)$; this measures displacement from the line in direction $\xi$.

A stage ends when a path first reaches $2n_*$ steps or changes its $r$ coordinate by at least $s_*$. Here $n_*,s_*>0$ are fixed length and width scales. A stage ending at one of these thresholds is full; the final shorter piece is a remainder.

The counted subpaths either exceed one of the two supporting linear bounds by $\eta s_*$, or cross a specified strip of length $n_*$ and half-width $8s_*$ with weight greater than $n_*g(\xi)-Ks_*$. Here $\eta,K>0$ are fixed constants. Disjointness concerns collected vertices, so a terminal vertex may be shared.
For a fixed threshold $M_0$, the correction on a path $\pi$ is $\sum_{z\text{ collected by }\pi}(\omega_z-M_0)^+$, where $a^+=\max\{a,0\}$.

coverage.scope: The one-step, stage and whole-path bounds include exactly the positive excess above the chosen cutoff, using the source witness maxima and connected block itinerary.

results.label: Lemma B.10
results.title: Bounding the contribution of large positive weights
results.summary: Almost surely, the total amount by which weights exceed a chosen threshold is eventually small on every sufficiently long connected collection of relevant blocks. This holds simultaneously for all such collections and therefore controls the correction for every long path.
definitions: A block is one of the overlapping rectangles used to contain a stage. Connected collections are joined by neighboring block indices; they need not be fixed before the weights are observed.

coverage.scope: The same original translated excess weights attain their maximum over the finite rooted animal family. The real limsup estimate and the path itinerary bound are certified.

results.label: Remark 4.3
results.title: Choosing short paths after observing low weights
results.summary: Deterministic short attachments need a stronger lower-tail estimate than the theorem assumes: under a power-law tail, their failure probability has an explicit lower bound. Selecting paths after locating very negative sites avoids this obstruction.
definitions: A level interval consists of the lattice points on $z_1+z_2=I$ between two specified endpoints, for an integer $I$.

coverage.scope: The general-weight replacement and its simultaneous connection conclusions are certified. The correspondence for this remark’s separate power-tail lower bound has not been independently checked here.

results.label: Remark 4.5
results.title: For fixed lengths, a direct tail bound suffices
results.summary: The integrated square-root upper-tail condition implies $t^2\mathbb P(\omega_0>t)→0$. For each fixed length, a union bound then rules out strip crossings that exceed a supporting value by a fixed multiple of the width.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Remark 4.6
results.title: The same bound for strips with any center
results.summary: The strip estimate of Proposition 4.4 extends to any integer starting level and any real center. Enlarging the half-width from $Rs$ to $(R+1)s$ absorbs the rounding used to place the strip inside a lattice translate of an origin-centered strip.
definitions: Here $s\ge1$ is the width scale and $R>0$ is fixed. The strip's center is measured in the coordinate $r(z)=z_1-\xi_1(z_1+z_2)$ for a fixed interior direction $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Remark 4.7
results.title: The same rarity with the shape threshold
results.summary: When the length is much larger than the strip width, the crossing threshold may be written using $g$ of the actual displacement. The supporting-line formulation retains the transverse contribution needed for uniformity.

coverage.scope: The two threshold formulations are certified in the regime where length divided by width tends to infinity. The level-only threshold warning is explanatory, without a claimed quantified counterexample.

results.label: Remark 6.1
results.title: Which connections require changes for unbounded weights
results.summary: The arbitrary-endpoint bound holds for both bounded and unbounded weights. The general proof uses random paths avoiding very negative weights, with endpoint adjustments controlled in Appendix B.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Remark 6.2
results.title: The connecting paths are shorter than the proof needs
results.summary: The deterministic connecting paths have at most $16C_*s_k$ steps. The proof retains the weaker bound $8C_*k^2s_k$ because it already yields the needed probability estimates; the sharper length observation is not needed for the differentiability conclusion.
definitions: Here $s_k=2^k$, and $C_*=50/\min\{\xi_1,1-\xi_1\}$ for the fixed interior direction $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$.

coverage.scope: The sharper length bound follows from the checked arithmetic and the printed staircase length estimate. The proof may retain its coarser bound.

results.label: Remark 6.3
results.title: Choose the connecting paths after locating negative weights
results.summary: The general-weight connection statement allows paths chosen from the locations of very negative sites. All selected paths avoid collecting those sites and satisfy a simultaneous lower weight bound.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Remark 6.4
results.title: The weight error on a short connecting interval
results.summary: On short grid intervals, the connection follows a path chosen to avoid very negative sites. Its lower weight estimate controls the difference between its weight and either supporting linear value.
definitions: The error scale is $t_k=\varepsilon_0 2^k/k$, where $k\ge1$ is an integer and $\varepsilon_0>0$ is fixed. A supporting linear function is a linear upper bound for $g$ that agrees with $g$ at the direction under consideration.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Remark 6.5
results.title: Independent crossings with no very large weight
results.summary: The longer-interval construction uses independent crossings in disjoint rectangles. Requiring the weights in each rectangle to remain below the chosen threshold reduces the success probability by at most half. The probability that every trial fails therefore decreases exponentially in the number of trials.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Remark 6.6
results.title: The weight error when a crossing needs two connections
results.summary: On long grid intervals, a successful crossing is shortened by a bounded number of vertices and joined at both ends to paths avoiding very negative weights. The resulting connection stays in the required strip and has a controlled loss relative to either supporting linear value.
definitions: The error scale is $t_k=\varepsilon_0 2^k/k$, where $k\ge1$ is an integer and $\varepsilon_0>0$ is fixed. A supporting linear function is a linear upper bound for $g$ that agrees with $g$ at the direction under consideration.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Remark 6.7
results.title: The common good event for general weights
results.summary: Intersect the crossing events with the geometry, selected-path weight and upper-cap events. This gives one common event on which the general connections are available.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Remark 6.9
results.title: The grid statement with random endpoints
results.summary: For unbounded weights, the grid connections end on paths selected to avoid very negative sites. The source claims this only for the grid intervals used to reach or leave an endpoint in Proposition 6.11. That modified statement, rather than every prescribed line position, is certified.

coverage.scope: The eligible random-staircase path clause is certified with exactly the source endpoint windows. It does not claim the bounded theorem’s arbitrary prescribed line positions.

results.label: Remark 6.10
results.title: The general grid event still has high probability
results.summary: The same common event has failure probability at most $2\beta_J$ for all sufficiently large selected scales, where $\beta_J→0$. The three additional error probabilities vanish with the scale.

coverage.scope: The literal common event, its added geometry and cap conditions, and its stated failure bound are certified on the same record-scale witnesses.

results.label: Remark 6.12
results.title: Removing a few endpoint vertices preserves the path bound
results.summary: The general-weight all-endpoint estimate retains the conclusion of Proposition 6.11. It permits endpoint adjustments of a bounded number of steps, with negligible discarded weight at the required scale.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Remark 7.1
results.title: Choosing a scale for unbounded weights
results.summary: Discusses the parameter choice for unbounded weights, including a scale-dependent upper cutoff and the correction for weights above it. This is a parameter discussion rather than a separate theorem.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Remark 7.3
results.title: The cost of moving across a corner
results.summary: When the left and right slopes of $g$ differ, moving sideways contributes a positive loss relative to their average supporting function. The loss is proportional to the slope difference and to the sideways displacement. This is the quantitative step that makes a corner incompatible with long near-optimal paths.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Remark 7.5
results.title: The stage bound includes weights above the cutoff
results.summary: For unbounded weights, each one-step estimate and the resulting stage estimate acquire the exact positive excess above the chosen cutoff. Lemma B.9 supplies the corresponding bound.

coverage.scope: The exact excess correction in this remark is certified by Lemma B.9.

results.label: Remark 7.8
results.title: The large-weight correction stays small
results.summary: The positive moment estimate makes the accumulated contribution above the cutoff smaller than the loss forced by a putative corner. After combining this with the bound on counted high-weight subpaths, every long path still loses a positive amount per stage, contradicting the shape limit.

results.label: Example 8.1
results.title: A law with no finite uniform shape limit
results.summary: For every $0<p<1$, the example gives a weight law with finite negative moment of order $p$ but no finite uniform shape limit. Along infinitely many interior endpoints, the last-passage time divided by endpoint distance becomes arbitrarily negative.
definitions: The endpoints lie in a fixed cone bounded away from the coordinate axes. The uniform limit concerns all sufficiently distant lattice endpoints in that cone at once.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Remark B.2
results.title: How the selected-path probability bound is used
results.summary: Substituting the attachment and staircase parameters into the path-family weight estimate gives the required vanishing errors. The staircase substitution retains its logarithmic scale factor.

coverage.scope: The substitutions give the required vanishing polynomial and stretched-exponential errors. The staircase estimate retains its logarithmic correction.

results.label: Remark B.5
results.title: Why the attachment proof uses a moment above one
results.summary: The attachment union bound needs polynomial lower-tail decay supplied by a moment above one. Integrability alone gives a weaker vanishing tail test; a possible logarithmic-moment extension is left open.

coverage.scope: The stated polynomial-decay explanation and the first-moment tail test are certified. The possible logarithmic-moment weakening remains speculative.

results.label: Shape theorem (§2.2)
results.title: The directional shape and uniform approximation
results.summary: The limit-defined shape $g$ is finite, continuous, homogeneous and concave on $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ under the stated moments. The cited shape theorem also gives a uniform almost-sure approximation.

source.locator: Section 2.2, shape theorem and equation eq:shape

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: S1
results.title: Uniform approximation at translated starting points
results.summary: The almost-sure uniform shape approximation holds at every fixed lattice start; countably many starts can be placed on one probability-one event.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: S2
results.title: Uniform probabilities for deterministic endpoints
results.summary: The probability of a relative shape error larger than a fixed tolerance tends to zero uniformly over every ordered deterministic endpoint pair at large separation.

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: S3
results.title: The shape dominates the mean weight
results.summary: For every $z\in\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$, the shape is at least the mean weight times $\ell(z)$.

results.label: S4
results.title: Lipschitz continuity away from the axes
results.summary: The shape is Lipschitz on each compact subset of the open quadrant and, by homogeneity, on each closed interior cone. No Lipschitz conclusion at the axes is claimed.

results.label: Sublinear geodesic loss (§2.6)
results.title: A directional geodesic has sublinear weight loss
results.summary: Geodesics to lattice approximations of $n\xi$ have weight equal to the average supporting value up to $o(n)$.
definitions: For the fixed interior direction $\xi$, the two supporting linear functions are $f_-$ and $f_+$, and $f=(f_-+f_+)/2$.

source.locator: Path weights and supporting functionals; equation eq:geodesic-defect

results.label: Moment bounds (§8.1)
results.title: Where the moment bounds enter
results.summary: Avoiding very negative weights replaces deterministic short connections. Positive excess is controlled over connected collections of blocks. The cubic characteristic-length bound gives blocks with order $s^4$ vertices.

source.locator: Relaxing bounded weights; roles of the moment bounds

coverage.scope: The stated mathematical conclusion is certified at the final-draft scope.

results.label: Finite negative mean (§8.2)
results.title: A finite horizontal rate needs an integrable negative part
results.summary: For upper-bounded independent weights, a finite horizontal passage rate forces the negative part to have finite first moment.

source.locator: Lower tail moment assumption; finite-mean necessity

coverage.scope: For upper-bounded weights, finite horizontal passage rate forces a finite first negative moment; a finite shape gives the required rate.

results.label: Necessary upper tail (§8.3)
results.title: The endpoint bound forces a small upper tail
results.summary: The arbitrary-endpoint estimate forces the number of sites in a block times the probability of a weight of order its width to tend to zero. A single large collected starting vertex would violate that estimate.

source.locator: Upper tail moment assumption; necessary tail condition

coverage.scope: The necessary upper-tail conclusion is certified assuming the source endpoint probability limit, with the collected-start one-step convention.

results.label: Conditional cap (§8.3)
results.title: Conditional cap bound for shorter blocks
results.summary: Assume the characteristic lengths are eventually bounded by $s_k^\gamma$ at all sufficiently large indices. A positive moment of order $p>2$ with $p>1+\gamma$ controls large weights in the corresponding blocks; the global cap retains its logarithmic correction.
definitions: Here $s_k=2^k$ is the transverse width and $\Lambda_k$ is the actual characteristic length of Proposition 5.3. The premise bounds $\Lambda_k$ by $s_k^\gamma$ eventually for every index, where $\gamma>1$. The positive moment order $p$ is greater than two.

source.locator: Upper tail moment assumption; conditional block-cap estimate

coverage.scope: The improved eventual power bound is a premise. The checked cap estimate assumes both $p>2$ and $p>1+\gamma$, including all sufficiently large predecessor indices; it does not establish an improved characteristic length.

results.label: Conditional excess (§8.3)
results.title: The excess bound at a general aspect ratio
results.summary: For $p>2$ and blocks of longitudinal size at most $s^\gamma$, the proved excess envelope has orders $s^{(1+\gamma)/p}$ and $s^{2+\gamma-p}$. This displayed envelope is $o(s)$ exactly when $p>1+\gamma$; the statement does not prove necessity for the actual excess.
definitions: Here $s_k=2^k$ is the transverse width and $\Lambda_k$ is the actual characteristic length of Proposition 5.3. The premise bounds $\Lambda_k$ by $s_k^\gamma$ eventually for every index, where $\gamma>1$. The positive moment order $p$ is greater than two.

source.locator: Upper tail moment assumption; conditional excess envelope

coverage.scope: The general two-power excess envelope and its little-o threshold are certified conditionally on the stated aspect-ratio bound. Necessity is asserted only for this envelope.

results.label: Scaling heuristics (§8.3)
results.title: Heuristic characteristic lengths
results.summary: KPZ and Flory fluctuation predictions suggest shorter characteristic lengths and lower positive-moment thresholds. These exponent laws are heuristic and do not lower the proved moment requirement.

source.locator: Upper tail moment assumption; KPZ and Flory heuristics

coverage.scope: Heuristic or conjectural discussion. No certificate for the asserted exponent or exponential-growth law is claimed.

results.label: Clipped shapes (§8.3)
results.title: Upper truncation approximates the shape
results.summary: The shape for weights capped at $M$ lies below the original shape, with a uniform error controlled by the integrated square-root upper tail. This error tends to zero as $M→∞$.

source.locator: Upper tail moment assumption; clipped-shape comparison

coverage.scope: The actual capped marginal has the stated shape comparison and uniform tail error on the closed unit segment.

results.label: Differentiability after capping (§8.3)
results.title: Each fixed upper truncation is differentiable
results.summary: Each fixed capped law preserves the required lower moment and has all positive moments. The main theorem, together with the linear shape of a constant law, gives differentiability at every fixed cutoff.

source.locator: Upper tail moment assumption; differentiability at each cutoff

coverage.scope: Every fixed cutoff is covered. Nondegenerate clipped laws use the main theorem; constant laws use their exact linear shape.

results.label: Common modulus (§8.3)
results.title: A shared modulus would pass differentiability to the limit
results.summary: If the clipped shape profiles have one differentiability modulus uniform over cutoffs, their uniform shape limit is differentiable. Existence of this common modulus is an unestablished premise.

source.locator: Upper tail moment assumption; conditional common-modulus argument

coverage.scope: The implication is certified with a modulus shared over all cutoffs as an explicit premise. Existence of that common modulus remains unestablished.

results.label: Confined top paths (§8.4)
results.title: A confined all-top path is a near-optimal crossing
results.summary: In a flat direction, an all-top path has exactly the shape-predicted weight. If it also satisfies the strip constraint, the positive weight allowance makes it a crossing of the event used to define characteristic length.

source.locator: Exclusion of the flat segment; confined all-top paths

coverage.scope: This elementary implication uses the actual flat-set equality and the strip crossing definition.

results.label: Fixed strip extinction (§8.4)
results.title: All-top paths eventually die in a fixed strip
results.summary: In every fixed finite-width strip and at each fixed start level, sufficiently long confined paths eventually contain a collected site strictly below the top weight, almost surely.

source.locator: Exclusion of the flat segment; fixed-strip extinction

coverage.scope: The almost-sure fixed-strip extinction claim is certified at every fixed signed start level. It does not imply any exponential lifetime bound.

results.label: Exponential lifetime conjecture (§8.4)
results.title: Conjectured exponential length in flat directions
results.summary: The paper expects near-optimal crossing probabilities in interior flat directions to remain large up to lengths exponential in the width. This is conjectural; the cited symmetric-strip and contact-process results do not establish the claim for every tilted strip.

source.locator: Exclusion of the flat segment; conjectured exponential lifetime

coverage.scope: Heuristic or conjectural discussion. No certificate for the asserted exponent or exponential-growth law is claimed.
